warmup.q: A JDK proxy for interface Ledger { long balance(String a); default long total(String a, String b) { return balance(a) + balance(b); } } has a handler that logs each call and then does return method.invoke(target, args);. A caller runs proxy.total("ops", "fees"). How many calls does the handler log?
options: 2: balance twice, because default methods never reach the handler
warmup.why: total reaches the handler like any interface method. The handler then runs the default body on the target, where this is the target, so the two balance calls never pass through the proxy. Run the body with InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, args) instead and this is the proxy: the handler then logs 3 calls.

sections.h: Proxy.newProxyInstance generates a real class, and you can read it
sections.html:
Start by writing a proxy yourself. This class does, for one interface, what the JDK will do for any interface. It holds one InvocationHandler, an object with a single method invoke(proxy, method, args) that receives every call:

Java
final class HandProxy implements FxQuotes {
    private static final Method QUOTE;                      // 1. looked up once
    static {
        try {
            QUOTE = FxQuotes.class.getMethod("quoteMicros", String.class);
        } catch (NoSuchMethodException e) {
            throw new NoSuchMethodError(e.getMessage());
        }
    }

    private final InvocationHandler h;
    HandProxy(InvocationHandler h) { this.h = h; }

    @Override
    public long quoteMicros(String pair) {
        try {
            return (Long) h.invoke(this, QUOTE, new Object[]{pair});   // 2. box, ask the handler, unbox
        } catch (RuntimeException | Error e) {
            throw e;                                                  // 3. unchecked: as is
        } catch (Throwable t) {
            throw new UndeclaredThrowableException(t);                // 4. undeclared checked: wrapped
        }
    }
    // ...the same for spreadMicros, equals, hashCode and toString
}
Kotlin
class HandProxy(private val h: InvocationHandler) : KFxQuotes {
    override fun quoteMicros(pair: String): Long =
        try {
            h.invoke(this, QUOTE, arrayOf(pair)) as Long             // 2. box, ask the handler, unbox
        } catch (e: RuntimeException) {
            throw e                                                  // 3. unchecked: as is
        } catch (e: Error) {
            throw e
        } catch (t: Throwable) {
            throw UndeclaredThrowableException(t)                    // 4. undeclared checked: wrapped
        }
    // ...the same for spreadMicros, equals, hashCode and toString

    companion object {
        private val QUOTE = KFxQuotes::class.java.getMethod("quoteMicros", String::class.java)  // 1. once
    }
}

Each method finds its java.lang.reflect.Method once, puts the arguments in an Object[] (boxing turns the primitives into objects such as Long), asks the handler, and unboxes the answer. Writing that by hand for forty methods on six client interfaces is tedious and easy to get wrong, so the JDK writes it for you.

In Decorator and Proxy you passed a handler to Proxy.newProxyInstance. At that moment the JDK generated a class like HandProxy, for whatever interfaces you listed. Here is what ProxyAnatomy reports about it, on JDK 21 and JDK 25 alike:

class      public final jdk.proxy1.$Proxy0
extends    java.lang.reflect.Proxy, implements [interface ...ProxyAnatomy$FxQuotes]
module     jdk.proxy1, hidden: false
fields     [m0, m1, m2, m3, m4]
methods    [equals, hashCode, proxyClassLookup, quoteMicros, spreadMicros, toString]

The Proxy Javadoc promises most of this. A proxy class is final, extends java.lang.reflect.Proxy, and implements exactly the interfaces you passed, in the same order. Its name is unspecified, but names starting with $Proxy are reserved for proxy classes, and Proxy.isProxyClass recognizes it. The module jdk.proxy1 and the counter in $Proxy0 are implementation details.

Every generated method is HandProxy.quoteMicros, written directly in bytecode. This is quoteMicros(String) as JDK 25 generates it:

{GEN}

So every call loads the handler and the proxy, fetches the Method object that the static initializer looked up once (m0 to m2 are hashCode, equals and toString, then your interface methods), copies the arguments into a fresh Object[] (boxing primitives), and calls invoke. The result is cast back and unboxed. A null returned for a primitive return type becomes a NullPointerException at that unboxing step.

The exception table is the whole exception contract. Error and RuntimeException pass straight through, and so do checked exceptions that the interface method declares. Anything else gets wrapped in UndeclaredThrowableException. quoteMicros declares nothing, so its last entry is any.

The Kotlin twin prints the same shape for a Kotlin interface. Proxies are a JVM feature, and kotlinc's interfaces are ordinary JVM interfaces. Since JDK 23 the JDK's ProxyGenerator writes these classes with the ClassFile API; JDK 21 still used its internal copy of ASM, which is why the JDK 21 bytecode differs slightly in its exception handler.

try.title: Take a proxy apart
steps: Read ProxyAnatomy (or ProxyAnatomy.kt). Before running it, predict which of the five calls in part 2 reach the handler.
Run it. Check the class name, its fields and methods, and the list the handler saw.
Look at part 3: why do {FxQuotes, Audited} and {Audited, FxQuotes} get different class names?

code.title: ProxyAnatomy.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l04; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler; import java.lang.reflect.Modifier; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; /** What Proxy.newProxyInstance generates, which calls reach the handler, and how the class is cached. */ public class ProxyAnatomy { public interface FxQuotes { long quoteMicros(String pair); default long spreadMicros(String pair) { return quoteMicros(pair) / 1_000; } } public interface Audited { String auditId(); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> seen = new ArrayList<>(); InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, a) -> { seen.add(m.getDeclaringClass().getSimpleName() + "." + m.getName()); return switch (m.getName()) { case "quoteMicros" -> 1_084_250L; case "hashCode" -> 42; case "equals" -> proxy == a[0]; case "toString" -> "FxQuotes proxy"; default -> null; }; }; ClassLoader app = FxQuotes.class.getClassLoader(); FxQuotes q = (FxQuotes) Proxy.newProxyInstance(app, new Class<?>[]{FxQuotes.class}, h); // 1. the generated class Class<?> pc = q.getClass(); System.out.println("class " + Modifier.toString(pc.getModifiers()) + " " + pc.getName()); System.out.println("extends " + pc.getSuperclass().getName() + ", implements " + Arrays.toString(pc.getInterfaces())); System.out.println("module " + pc.getModule().getName() + ", hidden: " + pc.isHidden()); System.out.println("fields " + Arrays.stream(pc.getDeclaredFields()).map(f -> f.getName()).sorted().toList()); System.out.println("methods " + Arrays.stream(pc.getDeclaredMethods()).map(m -> m.getName()).sorted().toList()); // 2. which calls reach the handler q.quoteMicros("EURUSD"); q.toString(); q.hashCode(); q.equals(q); q.getClass(); System.out.println("handler saw " + seen); // 3. the class is cached per loader and per ordered interface list Object again = Proxy.newProxyInstance(app, new Class<?>[]{FxQuotes.class}, (p, m, a) -> 0L); Object ab = Proxy.newProxyInstance(app, new Class<?>[]{FxQuotes.class, Audited.class}, h); Object ba = Proxy.newProxyInstance(app, new Class<?>[]{Audited.class, FxQuotes.class}, h); System.out.println("same class for the same interface: " + (again.getClass() == pc)); System.out.println("{FxQuotes, Audited} -> " + ab.getClass().getName() + ", {Audited, FxQuotes} -> " + ba.getClass().getName()); } }

try.expect: public final jdk.proxy1.$Proxy0, extending java.lang.reflect.Proxy in module jdk.proxy1, with fields m0 to m4. The handler saw quoteMicros, Object.toString, Object.hashCode and Object.equals, but not getClass(). The same interface again gives the same class. The two orderings give $Proxy1 and $Proxy2, because the class implements its interfaces in the order you list them, so the cache keys on the order too.

video.title: A dynamic proxy: every call becomes one invoke with a Method and an Object array

sections.h: What reaches the handler, and what the handler owes the caller
sections.html:
Three methods of Object reach the handler: hashCode, equals and toString, with method.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class. The other public Object methods, such as getClass, wait and notify, are final, and the proxy doesn't override them. For hashCode and other no-argument methods, args is null, not an empty array.

What you do with equals matters. The tempting handler forwards everything:

Java
InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, args) -> m.invoke(target, args);   // equals too
Kotlin
val h = InvocationHandler { _, m, args -> m.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) }   // equals too

Now proxy.equals(proxy) asks target.equals(proxy), and the target has never heard of the proxy, so the answer is false. equals is no longer reflexive. The ObjectMethodsDemo shows the symptom: after listeners.add(proxy), listeners.remove(proxy) returns false and the listener stays registered. A HashSet happens to survive, because HashMap compares references with == before it calls equals. That's luck, not correctness. Answer equals and hashCode by proxy identity (proxy == args[0], System.identityHashCode(proxy)), or decide on purpose how two proxies compare.

The handler also owes the caller the right exceptions. The generated method rethrows unchecked exceptions and the checked exceptions its interface method declares. It wraps any other checked exception in UndeclaredThrowableException. Method.invoke adds a second layer: whatever the target throws arrives wrapped in InvocationTargetException. A handler must catch that and rethrow e.getCause(), or the caller sees UndeclaredThrowableException wrapping InvocationTargetException wrapping the real error.

Kotlin makes the first rule easy to trip over. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so a Kotlin interface method declares none unless you write @Throws. A Kotlin implementation may still throw IOException (from a Java HTTP client it calls, say), because Kotlin doesn't check. A correctly unwrapping handler then produces UndeclaredThrowableException, and a Kotlin catch (e: IOException) around the call never matches. The demo's status() shows it. Add @Throws(IOException::class) to interface methods whose implementations throw checked exceptions.

Two more rules from the Javadoc. Only interfaces can be proxied: passing a class fails with IllegalArgumentException: ... is not an interface. And if two interfaces declare the same method, the handler gets the Method from the first interface in your list, whichever reference type the caller used.

try.title: Break equals, then the exception contract
steps: Run ObjectMethodsDemo (or the Kotlin twin) and read the four lines.

In forwardingEverything, answer equals before the try: if (m.getName().equals("equals")) return proxy == args[0]; (in Kotlin, if (m.name == "equals") return@newProxyInstance proxy === args[0]). Run it again.
In the Kotlin twin, remove @Throws(IOException::class) from authorize and predict what the catch (e: IOException) block does now. Run it.

code.title: ObjectMethodsDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l04; import java.io.IOException; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.lang.reflect.UndeclaredThrowableException; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; /** Two handler bugs: forwarding equals to the target, and throwing a checked exception the method doesn't declare. */ public class ObjectMethodsDemo { public interface IssuerClient { String authorize(String pan) throws IOException; // declares IOException String status(); // declares nothing } static class RealIssuer implements IssuerClient { public String authorize(String pan) throws IOException { throw new IOException("issuer timed out after 120 ms"); } public String status() { return "UP"; } } static IssuerClient forwardingEverything(IssuerClient target) { return (IssuerClient) Proxy.newProxyInstance(IssuerClient.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{IssuerClient.class}, (proxy, m, args) -> { try { return m.invoke(target, args); // equals and hashCode go to the target too } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); } }); } public static void main(String[] args) { IssuerClient p = forwardingEverything(new RealIssuer()); System.out.println("p.equals(p): " + p.equals(p) + " (target.equals(p) was asked)"); List<IssuerClient> listeners = new ArrayList<>(); listeners.add(p); System.out.println("listeners.remove(p) after listeners.add(p): " + listeners.remove(p) + ", size still " + listeners.size()); Set<IssuerClient> set = new HashSet<>(listeners); System.out.println("HashSet.contains(p): " + set.contains(p) + " (HashMap checks == before equals)"); try { p.authorize("4111111111111111"); } catch (IOException e) { System.out.println("declared IOException passes through: " + e.getMessage()); } IssuerClient angry = (IssuerClient) Proxy.newProxyInstance(IssuerClient.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{IssuerClient.class}, (proxy, m, a) -> { throw new IOException("connection reset"); }); try { angry.status(); } catch (UndeclaredThrowableException e) { System.out.println("undeclared IOException from status() -> UndeclaredThrowableException, cause: " + e.getCause()); } } }

alt.title: ObjectMethodsDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.bytecode.l04 import java.io.IOException import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException import java.lang.reflect.Proxy import java.lang.reflect.UndeclaredThrowableException interface KIssuerClient { @Throws(IOException::class) fun authorize(pan: String): String // @Throws writes `throws IOException` into the class file fun status(): String // Kotlin declares nothing unless you say so } class RealKIssuer : KIssuerClient { override fun authorize(pan: String): String = throw IOException("issuer timed out after 120 ms") override fun status() = "UP" } fun forwardingEverything(target: KIssuerClient): KIssuerClient = Proxy.newProxyInstance(KIssuerClient::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(KIssuerClient::class.java)) { _, m, args -> try { m.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) // equals and hashCode go to the target too } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! } } as KIssuerClient /** Two handler bugs: forwarding equals to the target, and throwing a checked exception the method doesn't declare. */ fun main() { val p = forwardingEverything(RealKIssuer()) println("p.equals(p): ${p.equals(p)} (target.equals(p) was asked)") val listeners = ArrayList<KIssuerClient>() listeners += p println("listeners.remove(p) after listeners.add(p): ${listeners.remove(p)}, size still ${listeners.size}") val set = HashSet(listeners) println("HashSet.contains(p): ${p in set} (HashMap checks == before equals)") try { p.authorize("4111111111111111") } catch (e: IOException) { println("declared IOException passes through: ${e.message}") } val angry = Proxy.newProxyInstance(KIssuerClient::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(KIssuerClient::class.java)) { _, _, _ -> throw IOException("connection reset") } as KIssuerClient try { angry.status() } catch (e: UndeclaredThrowableException) { println("undeclared IOException from status() -> UndeclaredThrowableException, cause: ${e.cause}") } }

try.expect: First run: p.equals(p): false, listeners.remove(p) ... false, size still 1, HashSet.contains(p): true, the declared IOException passing through, and UndeclaredThrowableException for status(). After the equals fix, p.equals(p) is true and remove works. Without @Throws, the Kotlin authorize call ends the program with an UndeclaredThrowableException whose cause is the IOException: the catch no longer matches.

sections.h: Default methods: the handler decides who this is
sections.html:
Decorator and Proxy showed the self-invocation trap: when the target calls this.authorize() inside its own method, this is the target, and the proxy never sees the inner call. Default methods give you a choice about that.

If the handler forwards a default method with method.invoke(target, args), the default body runs on the target. Its this is the target, and its inner calls skip the proxy. DefaultMethodsDemo logs [totalMinor].

JDK 16 added InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, args). It runs the interface's default body with this set to the proxy, so every call the body makes comes back through the handler:

Java
if (method.isDefault()) {
    return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, args);   // body runs with this = proxy
}
Kotlin
if (method.isDefault) {
    return@InvocationHandler InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, *(args ?: emptyArray()))
}

Now the demo logs [totalMinor, balanceMinor, balanceMinor]. The proxy doesn't even need a target: a handler that answers the abstract methods itself and sends defaults to invokeDefault is a complete implementation. Calling invokeDefault on an abstract method throws IllegalArgumentException, and on a default method your code can't access it throws IllegalAccessException.

Kotlin interfaces work too. With the labs' JVM target 21, kotlinc 2.4.21 compiles an interface function that has a body to a real JVM default method, plus a DefaultImpls class for older callers. method.isDefault is true and invokeDefault runs the Kotlin body (the Kotlin twin prints the same three calls).

This choice decides whether a retry proxy is safe. Take default String authorizeAndCapture(pan, amount) { return capture(authorize(pan, amount)); }. Suppose your handler treats it like any other method and retries it whenever it fails. The first attempt authorizes, then the capture fails, so the handler retries the whole method, and the second attempt sends another authorization to the issuer. Run defaults through invokeDefault and retry only the abstract calls inside them. A failed capture is then retried as a capture, and the authorization that already succeeded stays at one. The lab tests exactly this.

try.title: Count the handler calls
steps: Read DefaultMethodsDemo. Predict the handler saw list for both runs and the total for the target-less proxy.
Change RealLedger.balanceMinor to throw IllegalStateException for "fees" and run again. What does the first run's log contain when it fails?

code.title: DefaultMethodsDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l04; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException; import java.lang.reflect.Method; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Who is `this` inside a default method? It decides which inner calls the handler sees. */ public class DefaultMethodsDemo { public interface Ledger { long balanceMinor(String account); default long totalMinor(String a, String b) { // calls balanceMinor twice, on `this` return balanceMinor(a) + balanceMinor(b); } } static class RealLedger implements Ledger { public long balanceMinor(String account) { return account.length() * 1_000L; } } /** Logs every call it sees. Default methods go either to the target or through invokeDefault. */ static Ledger logging(Ledger target, boolean useInvokeDefault, List<String> log) { InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, args) -> { log.add(m.getName()); if (useInvokeDefault && m.isDefault()) { return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, args); // the body runs with this = proxy } try { return m.invoke(target, args); // the body runs with this = target } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); } }; return (Ledger) Proxy.newProxyInstance(Ledger.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{Ledger.class}, h); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { List<String> log = new ArrayList<>(); long t = logging(new RealLedger(), false, log).totalMinor("ops", "fees"); System.out.println("forward to target: total=" + t + ", handler saw " + log); log.clear(); t = logging(new RealLedger(), true, log).totalMinor("ops", "fees"); System.out.println("invokeDefault: total=" + t + ", handler saw " + log); // no implementation class at all: the handler answers balanceMinor, the interface supplies totalMinor Ledger noTarget = (Ledger) Proxy.newProxyInstance(Ledger.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{Ledger.class}, (proxy, m, a) -> m.isDefault() ? InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, a) : 500L); System.out.println("no target: total=" + noTarget.totalMinor("x", "y")); try { Method abstractOne = Ledger.class.getMethod("balanceMinor", String.class); InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(noTarget, abstractOne, "x"); } catch (Throwable e) { System.out.println("invokeDefault on an abstract method -> " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()); } } }

Default methods go either to the target or through invokeDefault. */ fun logging(target: KLedger, useInvokeDefault: Boolean, log: MutableList<String>): KLedger = Proxy.newProxyInstance(KLedger::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(KLedger::class.java)) { proxy, m, args -> log += m.name if (useInvokeDefault && m.isDefault) { InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, *args) // the body runs with this = proxy } else { try { m.invoke(target, *args) // the body runs with this = target } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! } } } as KLedger /** Who is `this` inside a default method? It decides which inner calls the handler sees. */ fun main() { val log = mutableListOf<String>() var t = logging(RealKLedger(), false, log).totalMinor("ops", "fees") println("forward to target: total=$t, handler saw $log") log.clear() t = logging(RealKLedger(), true, log).totalMinor("ops", "fees") println("invokeDefault: total=$t, handler saw $log") // no implementation class at all: the handler answers balanceMinor, the interface supplies totalMinor val noTarget = Proxy.newProxyInstance(KLedger::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(KLedger::class.java)) { proxy, m, a -> if (m.isDefault) InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, *a) else 500L } as KLedger println("no target: total=${noTarget.totalMinor("x", "y")}") try { InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(noTarget, KLedger::class.java.getMethod("balanceMinor", String::class.java), "x") } catch (e: Throwable) { println("invokeDefault on an abstract method -> ${e.javaClass.simpleName}") } }

try.expect: forward to target: total=7000, handler saw [totalMinor], then invokeDefault: total=7000, handler saw [totalMinor, balanceMinor, balanceMinor], then no target: total=1000 (two answers of 500), then IllegalArgumentException. With the exception for "fees", the program stops in the first run. Its stack trace shows RealLedger.balanceMinor called from Ledger.totalMinor on the target, and the handler never logged a balanceMinor: a retry or a timer in the handler couldn't have seen the failing call. In the invokeDefault version the same failure would pass through the handler as the second balanceMinor call.

sections.h: One class per loader and interface list, and a few nanoseconds per call
sections.html:
Generating a class is the expensive part, and the JDK does it once. Proxy caches proxy constructors per class loader, keyed by the ordered interface list. Ten thousand newProxyInstance calls with the same loader and interfaces generate one class and construct ten thousand small objects. Listing the same interfaces in a different order generates a second class, as ProxyAnatomy showed.

Each class loader gets one dynamic module for its proxies. On the runs for this track, proxies for app-loader interfaces landed in jdk.proxy1, and a Runnable proxy created with the bootstrap loader (null) landed in jdk.proxy2. If any interface is package-private, the proxy class goes into that interface's package instead, and it isn't public (demo.$Proxy8 in one run). Calling Constructor.newInstance on a proxy class in a dynamic module throws IllegalAccessException. Use newProxyInstance, because Proxy.getProxyClass is deprecated.

The per-call cost is the bytecode from section 1: an Object[], boxing, a virtual call to the handler, and whatever the handler does. One JMH run on JDK 25 (4 vCPUs, one fork, wide error bars) measured add(3, 4) like this:

Call ns/op
direct 0.83
Byte Buddy subclass with @SuperCall (lesson 5) 0.88
JDK proxy, handler calls method.invoke(target, args) 4.3
plain Method.invoke with boxing 11.8

Read the order, not the decimals. A few nanoseconds per call is nothing next to a 120 ms issuer call or a database round trip. It does show up in a loop that calls a proxied interface millions of times, and there a subclass proxy or plain code wins.

You can save the generated class and read it yourself. -Djdk.proxy.ProxyGenerator.saveGeneratedFiles=true writes it to jdk/proxy1/$Proxy0.class under the current directory. On JDK 21 that just works. On the JDK 24, 25, 26 and 27 builds tested for this track, the JDK writes the first file and then newProxyInstance throws NullPointerException. The JDK source explains it: a return null; that used to sit inside a doPrivileged lambda now returns from generateProxyClass itself. The file is still written, so you can read it on any of them.

try.title: Read the class the JDK wrote
steps: Run ProxyAnatomy once with Gradle so its classes exist. Then, from labs/, run the commands below. They work in a temporary directory, because the flag writes into the current one.
On JDK 24 or later, expect a NullPointerException after the first file is written. Carry on with javap.
Find quoteMicros and compare it with the listing in section 1. Then find the static initializer: where does it look up m3?

code.title: terminal
code.html: D=$PWD/bytecode/build/classes/java/demo cd "$(mktemp -d)" java -Djdk.proxy.ProxyGenerator.saveGeneratedFiles=true -cp "$D" workbench.bytecode.l04.ProxyAnatomy javap -c -p 'jdk/proxy1/$Proxy0.class' | less

try.expect: quoteMicros loads h, the proxy and m3, builds a one-element Object[], calls InvocationHandler.invoke, then checkcast Long and longValue. The static initializer calls Class.getMethod for hashCode, equals, toString, quoteMicros and spreadMicros (on JDK 21 it first loads each class with Class.forName) and stores them in m0 to m4. On JDK 21 the program also prints its normal output. On JDK 24 and later it stops with the NPE after writing $Proxy0.class.

analogy: A JDK proxy is a receptionist for a list of phone extensions. Every call to one of those extensions goes to the receptionist, who writes a note (the Method and an Object[] of arguments) and hands it to one person, the handler, who decides what happens. Calls that staff make to each other inside the office never pass reception, which is self-invocation. A default method is a script taped to the desk: the handler can give the script to a staff member to read (forward it to the target), or read it out at reception itself (invokeDefault), in which case every call the script makes goes through reception again. The analogy breaks on identity. A receptionist knows they aren't the person you asked for, but a careless handler that forwards equals makes the proxy deny being itself.
world: Payments code proxies interfaces all the time without saying so: REST clients, Kafka producer wrappers and repository interfaces in many frameworks are interfaces with a generated implementation behind them. A JDK proxy like the lab's is the right tool when you own the interface, for example a CardIssuerClient that every issuer adapter implements, and you want one retry, timeout and metrics policy around all of them. Be strict about what you retry: an authorization or a capture is safe to repeat only with an idempotency key the issuer deduplicates on. And keep equals honest: a proxied listener registered in a list that can't be removed is a memory leak that grows with every deploy-time reload.
mistake: The most common mistake is a handler that treats every Method the same way. It forwards equals, hashCode and toString to the target, which breaks reflexivity, so collections can't find or remove the proxy. It forwards or retries default methods as one unit, so their inner calls skip the retry and timing logic, or the whole sequence runs again. And it lets InvocationTargetException escape, so callers get UndeclaredThrowableException. People write it that way because the one-line m.invoke(target, args) handler works in the first test. The fix is a handler with four explicit cases in order: Object methods, default methods (invokeDefault), the methods you decorate, and an unwrapping catch.

compare.title: A tracing proxy in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Tracing.java
java.html: @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") static <T> T tracing(Class<T> iface, T target, List<String> log) { InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, args) -> { if (m.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class) { // 1. identity, not the target's return switch (m.getName()) { case "equals" -> proxy == args[0]; case "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy); default -> "Tracing[" + target + "]"; }; } log.add(m.getName()); if (m.isDefault()) return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, args); // 2. this = proxy try { return m.invoke(target, args); // 3. args is null for no-arg methods } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); // 4. the target's own exception } }; return (T) Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, h); }

kotlin.title: Tracing.kt
kotlin.html: inline fun <reified T : Any> tracing(target: T, log: MutableList<String>): T = Proxy.newProxyInstance(T::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(T::class.java)) { proxy, m, args -> val a = args ?: emptyArray() // 3. null for no-arg methods when { m.declaringClass == Any::class.java -> when (m.name) { // 1. identity "equals" -> proxy === a[0] "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy) else -> "Tracing[$target]" } else -> { log += m.name if (m.isDefault) InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, *a) // 2. this = proxy else try { m.invoke(target, *a) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! // 4. the target's own exception } } } } as T

compare.note: Same JVM mechanism, same four cases. The Kotlin version is shorter because reified T reads T::class.java itself, so callers write tracing(issuer, log). Two Kotlin-specific traps sit in it. args is a nullable Java array, null for methods with no parameters, so spreading it directly (*args) throws NullPointerException on hashCode(). And Kotlin interfaces declare no checked exceptions unless you add @Throws, so a Java client's IOException that the handler rethrows correctly still reaches Kotlin callers as UndeclaredThrowableException.

worked.title: A test double for CardIssuerClient with no implementation class

steps.say: A test needs a CardIssuerClient that returns canned answers and records what was called, and you don't want to write a class with every method. A proxy with no target can do it. Start with the cases every handler needs.
steps.code: static CardIssuerClient fakeIssuer(Map<String, Object> answers, List<String> calls) { InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, args) -> { // 1. Object methods: identity, so the fake behaves in collections if (m.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class) { return switch (m.getName()) { case "equals" -> proxy == args[0]; case "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy); default -> "FakeIssuer" + answers.keySet(); }; } // 2. default methods: run the real interface body, which calls back through this handler if (m.isDefault()) return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, args); // 3. abstract methods: record the call and return the canned answer calls.add(m.getName() + Arrays.toString(args)); if (!answers.containsKey(m.getName())) throw new UnsupportedOperationException(m.getName()); return answers.get(m.getName()); }; return (CardIssuerClient) Proxy.newProxyInstance( CardIssuerClient.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{CardIssuerClient.class}, h); }

alt.html: fun fakeIssuer(answers: Map<String, Any>, calls: MutableList<String>): CardIssuerClient = Proxy.newProxyInstance(CardIssuerClient::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(CardIssuerClient::class.java)) { proxy, m, args -> val a = args ?: emptyArray() when { // 1. Object methods: identity, so the fake behaves in collections m.declaringClass == Any::class.java -> when (m.name) { "equals" -> proxy === a[0] "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy) else -> "FakeIssuer${answers.keys}" } // 2. default methods: run the real interface body, which calls back through this handler m.isDefault -> InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, *a) // 3. abstract methods: record the call and return the canned answer else -> { calls += m.name + a.contentToString() answers[m.name] ?: throw UnsupportedOperationException(m.name) } } } as CardIssuerClient

steps.say: Use it. The interesting call is the default method: the fake has no code for authorizeAndCapture, yet the interface's own body runs and its two inner calls are recorded in order. That only works because of invokeDefault. Forwarding to a target isn't possible here, since there is no target.
steps.code: List<String> calls = new ArrayList<>(); CardIssuerClient issuer = fakeIssuer( Map.of("authorize", "auth-1111", "capture", "captured auth-1111"), calls); String result = issuer.authorizeAndCapture("4111111111111111", 1_250); // 4. exercise the default assertThat(result).isEqualTo("captured auth-1111"); assertThat(calls).containsExactly("authorize[4111111111111111, 1250]", "capture[auth-1111]");

alt.html: val calls = mutableListOf<String>() val issuer = fakeIssuer(mapOf("authorize" to "auth-1111", "capture" to "captured auth-1111"), calls) val result = issuer.authorizeAndCapture("4111111111111111", 1_250) // 4. exercise the default assertThat(result).isEqualTo("captured auth-1111") assertThat(calls).containsExactly("authorize[4111111111111111, 1250]", "capture[auth-1111]")

steps.say: Check the edges before you trust it. A canned answer of the wrong type fails at the proxy's checkcast, with a ClassCastException from the generated method rather than from your handler. A missing answer for a method returning long would be null, and the proxy's unboxing turns that into a NullPointerException, so the handler throws a clear UnsupportedOperationException instead. And the fake works for one interface only. Mocking libraries generalize the same idea, adding argument matchers and class support.

lab.title: A retrying, timing proxy for CardIssuerClient
steps: Run the tests once. All seven fail. Read CardIssuerClient and the FakeIssuer in the test: it fails a scripted number of calls and counts every one.
In ResilientProxy.wrap, create the proxy with Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, handler) and return iface.cast(...).
Write the handler's first two cases: Object methods answered by identity and "Resilient[" + target + "]", then default methods through InvocationHandler.invokeDefault.

Write the retry loop: read the clock once, call method.invoke(target, args), and on InvocationTargetException take getCause(). Retry while attempts are left and policy.retries(cause) is true. Record iface.getSimpleName() + "." + method.getName() with the attempt count and end - start once, when the call ends.
Run the tests until all seven pass. Then read defaultMethodShellIsNotRetried and say out loud why the issuer saw one authorization.
hints: The order of the cases matters. equals is not a default method, but check Object methods first anyway, so nothing else ever sees them.
The fake clock moves 5 ms per read. If the recorded time isn't 5ms, you're reading the clock more than twice per call.

throw cause; compiles because InvocationHandler.invoke is declared throws Throwable. Because the cause is the target's own exception, the generated method lets IssuerUnavailableException through: authorize declares it.

drill.title: The four cases from memory
drill.prompt: Close the page. Write an InvocationHandler that times each call of an interface and reports the method name, handling the four cases in the right order: Object methods, default methods, the timed call, and exceptions. Then check your version against the answer. Which case did you forget?

answer.html: InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, args) -> { if (m.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class) { // 1. Object methods return switch (m.getName()) { case "equals" -> proxy == args[0]; case "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy); default -> "Timed[" + target + "]"; }; } if (m.isDefault()) return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, args); // 2. defaults: this = proxy long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { return m.invoke(target, args); // 3. the timed call } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); // 4. unwrap } finally { metrics.record(m.getName(), System.nanoTime() - t0); } };

alt.html: val h = InvocationHandler { proxy, m, args -> val a = args ?: emptyArray() if (m.declaringClass == Any::class.java) { // 1. Object methods return@InvocationHandler when (m.name) { "equals" -> proxy === a[0] "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy) else -> "Timed[$target]" } } if (m.isDefault) return@InvocationHandler InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, *a) // 2. defaults val t0 = System.nanoTime() try { m.invoke(target, *a) // 3. the timed call } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! // 4. unwrap } finally { metrics.record(m.name, System.nanoTime() - t0) } }

recap: Proxy.newProxyInstance generates a public final $ProxyN extends Proxy that implements exactly your interfaces, in order. Each method boxes its arguments into an Object[] and calls h.invoke(proxy, Method, args).
hashCode, equals and toString reach the handler; getClass doesn't. Answer equals/hashCode by proxy identity, or collections can't find the proxy.

Unchecked exceptions and declared checked exceptions pass through; any other checked exception becomes UndeclaredThrowableException. Unwrap InvocationTargetException, and use @Throws on Kotlin interfaces.
InvocationHandler.invokeDefault (JDK 16) runs a default body with this = proxy, so its inner calls come back through the handler. Forwarding to the target hides them.
Never retry a default method as a whole: retry the abstract calls inside it, or a successful step runs twice.
Proxy classes are cached per loader and ordered interface list, in one jdk.proxyN module per loader. A call costs a few nanoseconds: irrelevant for I/O, visible in tight loops.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to wrap every issuer client in a JDK proxy that retries on timeouts. Explain what the JDK generates, the four cases their handler must handle, and the one retry rule that keeps a default method like authorizeAndCapture from charging twice.
explain.answer: Proxy.newProxyInstance generates one final class per class loader and interface list. Each of its methods boxes the arguments into an Object[] and calls the handler with the proxy and a cached Method. The handler must first answer equals, hashCode and toString itself, by proxy identity, or collections stop finding the proxy. Second, it must run default methods with InvocationHandler.invokeDefault, so the body runs with this as the proxy and each inner call comes back through the handler. Third, it calls the target with method.invoke and retries only failures the policy names, like a timeout. Fourth, it rethrows InvocationTargetException.getCause(), so callers get the issuer's own exception and not an UndeclaredThrowableException. The retry rule: never retry a default method as one unit. Retry the abstract calls inside it, so a failed capture is retried as a capture, and the authorization that already succeeded isn't sent again.

deeper.html:
Three corners of Proxy that the lesson skipped.

Modules and visibility. If every interface is public and in an exported package, the proxy class is public, in an unconditionally exported but non-open package of a dynamic module. If any interface is non-public, the proxy class is non-public and goes into that interface's package and module, so all non-public interfaces must share one package. If an interface is in a package its module doesn't export, the proxy goes into a non-exported package of a dynamic module. In every dynamic-module case, Constructor.newInstance on the proxy class throws IllegalAccessException, which is why Proxy.getProxyClass is deprecated.

What can fail at creation. newProxyInstance throws IllegalArgumentException when an element isn't a non-hidden, non-sealed interface, when an interface appears twice, when an interface isn't visible by name through the loader you pass (Class.forName(i.getName(), false, loader) != i), when two interfaces have a method with the same signature and incompatible return types, or when you pass more than 65,535 interfaces. The loader rule is the one you'll meet: in a Quarkus test or a plugin system, pass the loader that defined the interface (iface.getClassLoader()), not some other loader that has a second copy of it (lesson 1).

The caches. Proxy keeps the constructors in a ClassLoaderValue, so the cache entry goes away with the loader. A second cache backs isProxyClass. And a ClassValue of ConcurrentHashMap<Method, MethodHandle> holds the method handles behind invokeDefault, so only the first call of each default method pays for the lookup.

The saveGeneratedFiles crash from section 4 is easy to see in the source. At jdk-21-ga, generateProxyClass wrote the file inside AccessController.doPrivileged(new PrivilegedAction<>() { ... return null; }), and that return null belonged to the lambda. At jdk-24-ga, the release that permanently disabled the Security Manager, the doPrivileged wrapper is gone, and the same return null; now returns from generateProxyClass itself, so defineClass receives null bytes.
